source: Haynes et al. (2009) A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. NEJM 360:491
finding: Before-after study in 8 hospitals: a 19-item checklist, a task-structuring artifact used by the team, came with fewer deaths and complications.
numbers: 3733 patients before, 3955 after. Death 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003). Inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001).
limits: Abstract read via PubMed. No control group; before-after only. A checklist is a procedure aid, not the same as a speed bug. Not aviation.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: best direct evidence that a structured external artifact lowers error rates. Supports checklist-like gates (guardrails) but only observationally.

source: Pronovost et al. (2006) An intervention to decrease catheter-related bloodstream infections in the ICU. NEJM 355:2725
finding: A checklist-based evidence bundle in Michigan ICUs was followed by a large, sustained fall in infections.
numbers: 103 ICUs, 375,757 catheter-days. Median rate per 1000 catheter-days 2.7 to 0 at 3 months. Mean 7.7 to 1.4 at 16-18 months. Rate ratio 0.62 (0-3 mo) to 0.34 (16-18 mo).
limits: Abstract only. Cohort design, no concurrent control; the bundle included more than the checklist, so the artifact is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: second large positive before-after result for checklists. Effect cannot be credited to the card alone.

source: Urbach et al. (2014) Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada. NEJM 370:1029
finding: A natural experiment after mandatory checklist adoption found no significant gain: a failure to replicate the large Haynes effect in typical practice.
numbers: 101 hospitals, 109,341 procedures before and 106,370 after. Death 0.71% to 0.65% (OR 0.91, CI 0.80-1.03, P=0.13). Complications 3.86% to 3.82% (OR 0.97, P=0.29).
limits: Abstract only. Administrative data, 3-month windows, quality of use not observed. A mandate may mean box-ticking.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: artifacts help only when used as the work practice intends. A checklist an agent ticks without checking would be the Ontario case. Test use, not presence.

source: Gap search note: controlled tests of the cockpit speed bug or speed card against plain memory
finding: No controlled with-versus-without comparison of speed bugs or speed cards was found in the sources reachable this session. Web search was exhausted, so this is a weak negative.
limits: Only PubMed and arXiv endpoints were reached; aviation human-factors journals were not.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays partly open for aviation. The checklist trials (d01-d03) are the nearest quantitative evidence.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? arXiv 2503.13657 (v3)
finding: This is close to a cognitive ethnography of agent systems. Grounded-theory reading of 150+ traces built a failure taxonomy (MAST), then 1600+ traces were annotated across 7 frameworks.
numbers: Six expert annotators; kappa 0.88 on 15 traces; LLM annotator (o1) kappa 0.77, 0.79 on unseen systems, accuracy 94%.
limits: Taxonomy built by the authors; the LLM annotator agrees less than humans do. Frameworks and models are of 2024-25.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the method (read traces, name who held which state, code failures) is used on agents and gives a reusable codebook.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) MAST intervention case studies, Appendix H, Table 5
finding: Trace-guided fixes raised success modestly. Topology changes beat prompt changes on ChatDev; on AG2 results depended on the model.
numbers: ChatDev ProgramDev-v0 (32 tasks): baseline 25.0, improved prompts 34.4, new topology 40.6. HumanEval 89.6 / 90.3 / 91.5. AG2 GSM-Plus 200 problems, 6 runs: GPT-4 84.75+-1.94 / 89.75+-1.44 / 85.50+-1.18; GPT-4o 84.25 / 89.00 / 88.83. Topology gain on GPT-4 not significant (Wilcoxon p=0.4); GPT-4o p=0.03.
limits: Tokens were not matched. The cyclic topology and added verification step add calls. The paper itself calls the gains not substantial. One group of authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: trace coding did lead to design changes with gains of 5-15 points, but equal-token accuracy is unreported, so the gap is only half closed.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When) arXiv 2505.00212
finding: LLMs are poor at the ethnographer's job of saying which agent and step caused a failure in a trace.
numbers: 127 multi-agent systems' failure logs. Best method 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level accuracy. Some methods below random. o1 and DeepSeek-R1 also not practically usable.
limits: Benchmark of failure logs from hand-built and generated systems; the task is hard even for humans.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: an agent cannot yet auto-diagnose its own trace reliably, so a trace-reading step in the schema needs a human or an external check.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR. arXiv 2310.01798
finding: Without outside feedback, a second pass changes right answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse, so self-verification can flip or lock onto the first answer.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K reaches 84.3 (a leak). GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: LLM verifying itself, not a human verifying an LLM as in Shen. Older models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2). Result depends on the prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a verification step is safe only if it uses a different signal (tests, retrieval, another model). Self-review with the same context is not.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Can Vision-Language Models Analyze Human-Centered Videos? Section 6.3.1 and discussion item 11. arXiv 2609.27327
finding: Verification hurt where the VLM was already accurate on precise boundaries (behaviour intervals, animal behaviour). The paper warns that reviewers can anchor on a plausible VLM output.
numbers: Behaviour interval HNS 101.6 to 86.5; animal behaviour 110.8 to 90.5. Verification raised human-human agreement on 11 of 15 tasks (workflow reconstruction 0.761 to 0.925).
quote: A plausible VLM output can increase agreement by anchoring reviewers on the same interpretation without increasing accuracy.
limits: Anchoring is the authors' reading, not tested directly; no condition hides the VLM label on the same task. One VLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: higher agreement after seeing a first pass is not evidence of validity. Anchoring is plausible, mainly on boundary tasks, and untested.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems. arXiv 2512.08296 (v3)
finding: With matched tools and total reasoning-token budget (mean 4,800 tokens per trial), multi-agent gains depend on task type and can be large losses.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks. Range +80.8% (finance, centralized) to -70.0% (PlanCraft planning, independent). Planning -39% to -70% for all multi-agent variants. Single agent above about 45% accuracy gets negative returns from more agents. Independent agents amplify errors 17.2x, centralized 4.4x. Web navigation decentralized +9.2%. Cross-validated R2 0.373.
limits: Matched total budget favours single agents on tool-heavy work by design. Frontier models and tasks of 2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: at equal tokens multi-agent is not a general win. A single agent with role switching is the safe default; add a centralised check only for decomposable tasks.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate. arXiv 2502.08788 (v3)
finding: Five debate methods across 9 benchmarks and 4 models often failed to beat plain chain of thought or self-consistency, despite more compute.
numbers: 5 methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 models. Where self-consistency applies it was usually the top method; debate was a less efficient use of tokens.
limits: Debate, not role pipelines like MetaGPT. Per-benchmark tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: debate-style multi-agent gain does not survive equal compute against sampling plus voting.

source: Shang et al. (2026) United Minds or Isolated Agents? CoThinker under Cognitive Load Theory. TMLR, arXiv 2506.06843 (v3)
finding: The published v3 reports the CoThinker gain with bootstrap SEs and Holm tests. The gain is real against single agents but not shown at equal tokens.
numbers: Gains on LiveBench subtasks about +5.1 (Reasoning vs CoT), +5.3 (Data vs IO), +6.0 (Language vs SR), p<.001 to 0.001. 16 of 25 comparisons clear Holm at 0.05; the 3 significant losses are instruction-following. Output tokens per question (Flash): IO 638, CoT 643, MAD 16,104, CoThinker 14,323; API calls 1 vs 25.
limits: Tokens are matched to debate baselines (0.89-1.11x MAD), not to single-agent CoT, so about 22x more output than CoT. A constrained 8,192-token run exists (Gemini-2.5 Math 76.3 vs 59.3 IO) but no self-consistency at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 7: the +5 to +6 point result is verified in the paper text; its equal-token advantage is not shown.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning. arXiv 2303.11366 (v4)
finding: Reflection ablations are scored on task success, not rater ranking. Self-reflection beat plain episodic memory on HotPotQA reasoning.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. HotPotQA ablation (100 questions): reflection adds about 8% absolute over episodic memory alone.
limits: Same-lab result, 100-question ablation, repeated attempts at the same task with ground-truth signals. Not a replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: task-success evidence for reflection exists, but it needs an external signal such as tests. Compare d08.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following. arXiv 2505.16067 (v2)
finding: An independent lab studied memory effects on agent behaviour and found agents copy similar past records, so bad stored experience propagates.
numbers: Abstract and section scan only; exact accuracy deltas not extracted. Reports error propagation and misaligned experience replay, and that filtering stored records helps.
limits: Numbers not extracted. Agents and tasks chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: memory writes need a quality gate. Raters' believability (Park 2023) is not task success.

source: Toubia et al. (2025) Twin-2K-500: digital twins of 2,058 people. arXiv 2505.17479
finding: A second lab with a test-retest benchmark finds twins good on survey items; the data include trust and dictator games.
numbers: N=2,058, 4 waves, 500 questions. Mean accuracy 71.72% over 17 tasks; 87.67% of test-retest accuracy (GPT-4.1-mini, text persona).
limits: Per-game breakdown not extracted. One model family.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: persona simulation reaches about 88% of retest on average. I did not confirm game-level failure on newer models.

source: Park et al. (2024) Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People (earlier version in local text; later version in c15). arXiv 2411.10109
finding: In the earlier text, incentivised economic games showed no significant gain from interview grounding.
numbers: Normalised correlation: interview 0.66, persona 0.57, demographic 0.48, survey-plus-interview 0.49, survey 0.38. ANOVA F(4,5255)=1.63, p=0.16. Same text: GSS normalised accuracy 0.83 (raw 65.67%); Big Five 0.80.
limits: Earlier version; the later version gives other figures (see c15, 1,052 people). No newer-model rerun found.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays partly open: interviews help stated attitudes but not paid decisions in both versions. Reason unconfirmed.

source: Chew et al. (2023) LLM-Assisted Content Analysis (LACA). arXiv 2306.14924
finding: GPT-3.5 matched human agreement on many deductive codes but guessed on some, and gave hallucinated reasons.
numbers: 4 public datasets, 100 docs each. Trump Tweets: 4 of 13 codes not different from random (HSTG p=0.193, ATSN 0.920, CAPT 0.764, INDV 0.193). Gwet AC1 used.
limits: Closed codebooks; GPT-3.5; not open or inductive coding. No count of invented categories.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: for a closed codebook a randomness test finds the codes the LLM cannot do. Open-codebook kappa and invented-category rates remain unmeasured here.

source: Xiao et al. (2023) Supporting Qualitative Analysis with LLMs: Codebook with GPT-3 for Deductive Coding. arXiv 2304.10548
finding: GPT-3 with an expert codebook reached fair to substantial agreement with experts on curiosity-driven questions.
numbers: Cohen kappa fair to substantial (values per code not extracted).
limits: Deductive only, davinci-002; abstract and setup scanned only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: confirms the closed-codebook picture. No open-codebook evidence found; the gap stays open.

source: Hutchins project page: Ship navigation (publication list incl. Seifert and Hutchins 1992 Error as opportunity)
finding: The page lists the primary ship-navigation papers (Organizing work by adaptation 1991; Technology of team navigation 1990; Seifert and Hutchins 1992) but gives no numbers. The book was not opened.
numbers: No team size, fix-cycle or error counts retrievable here.
limits: Search was exhausted, so no replication search was possible. Seifert and Hutchins 1992 reports error analysis but its text was not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. Treat Cognition in the Wild numbers as unverified.
